cards.title: Event Storming: Brandolini's Invention
cards.teaser: Event Storming is a collaborative modeling workshop invented by Alberto Brandolini in 2013. In a single room — or a shared virtual canvas — developers, domain experts, and product owners build a shared picture of a business domain faster than any requirements document could.

runs.text: Alberto Brandolini, an Italian software craftsman, first described Event Storming publicly in 2013 after years of experimenting with workshop formats that could bridge the gap between domain experts and software teams. He formalized the technique in his book
Introducing EventStorming

(Leanpub, 2017). The name fuses Domain Events (the core DDD concept) with the word "storming" — from brainstorming — because the workshop is intentionally chaotic and generative before it becomes structured.
The core premise is deceptively simple: cover a long wall with paper, hand everyone a stack of orange sticky notes, and ask them to write down
things that happen

in the business — one event per sticky, written in past tense. "Order Placed", "Payment Declined", "Shipment Dispatched". These events are then arranged left-to-right on a timeline. What emerges in 90 minutes is a shared model that no one person could have produced alone.

Event Storming works because it forces the right people into the same room with a shared artifact to argue over. The sticky notes are not the product — the conversations triggered by placing, moving, and challenging them are. Brandolini has called it "the highest ROI activity in software development" because it surfaces domain confusion, missing concepts, and bounded context boundaries in hours rather than months.

Event Storming is tool-agnostic: it was designed for physical rooms with real sticky notes, but is regularly run on virtual canvases using Miro, Mural, or EventModeler. The mechanics translate directly; the social dynamics require more deliberate facilitation in remote settings.

Event Storming is a workshop where everyone who knows the business and everyone who will build the software write important business events on sticky notes, stick them on a timeline, and argue about the order — and the arguing is the point.

cards.title: The Orange Sticky: Domain Events
cards.teaser: Orange stickies are the foundation of Event Storming. Each one captures a domain event — something that happened in the business that the domain experts care about — written in past tense. Every other element in the workshop is there to explain why or how orange stickies occur.

runs.text: The orange sticky note represents a
Domain Event
: a fact about something that happened that is relevant to the business. The grammar rule is strict: past tense, noun phrase, written from the domain's perspective — not from a technical perspective.

items.text: Correct:
"Order Placed", "Payment Failed", "Account Suspended", "Shipment Delayed"
Incorrect:
"Insert order into DB", "Call payment API", "Update status field" — these are implementation, not domain events.

runs.text: Domain events are placed left-to-right on the timeline in the order they occur during a business process. When two participants place conflicting events — or place the same event in different positions — that divergence is a signal, not an error. It means the domain experts have different mental models, and the workshop has just surfaced something that would otherwise have caused a production bug in month six.

A healthy Event Storming session starts with a divergent explosion of orange stickies — 50, 80, 150 — then converges as duplicates are collapsed and sequences clarified. The volume of orange stickies at peak is a measure of how much domain knowledge was previously implicit.

Brandolini's rule of thumb: if a domain event does not matter to the business or a domain expert does not recognize it, it should not be on the wall. Technical events like "Record Saved" or "Cache Invalidated" are not domain events.
An orange sticky means "this thing happened" — written in past tense from the business's point of view. "Order Placed" is a domain event. "Row inserted in orders table" is not.

cards.title: The Blue Sticky: Commands
cards.teaser: Blue stickies represent commands — the explicit intentions or decisions that cause domain events to occur. Where an orange sticky says what happened, a blue sticky says what someone decided to do. Together they form the cause-and-effect chain of a business process.

runs.text: A
Command

is a request to do something — an imperative, issued by a user, another system, or a policy. Commands are written in the imperative mood, present tense: "Place Order", "Decline Payment", "Suspend Account". A command is always placed to the
left
of the event it causes on the timeline.
The command-event pair is the atomic unit of causation in Event Storming:

explanation.text:
[Blue: Place Order] --> [Orange: Order Placed]
[Blue: Decline Payment] --> [Orange: Payment Declined]
[Blue: Suspend Account] --> [Orange: Account Suspended]

runs.text: Not every event needs to be preceded by an explicit user command. Events can also be caused by policies ("When payment fails three times, suspend account") or external systems ("Payment gateway reports timeout"). But for most user-facing flows, identifying the command makes the actor visible — who or what decided to trigger this chain of consequences?

Commands are often the first place that disputes about scope appear. "Who is allowed to cancel an order after it has shipped?" The question sounds like a business rule, but it is really a question about which actor can issue which command under which conditions. Making commands explicit forces that conversation.
A blue sticky is the "please do this" that precedes the orange "this happened". "Place Order" (blue) causes "Order Placed" (orange). Commands are the intentions; events are the results.

cards.title: The Yellow Sticky: Aggregates
cards.teaser: Yellow stickies represent aggregates — the clusters of domain objects that enforce business invariants. In Event Storming, an aggregate is the thing that receives a command, applies business rules, and emits a domain event. Yellow stickies appear between blue and orange on the timeline.

runs.text: In design-level Event Storming, once commands and events are established, the team asks: "What business object is responsible for deciding whether this command is valid?" That object is the
aggregate
. A yellow sticky is placed between the blue command and the orange event it produces, representing the aggregate that enforces the invariant.
The full causal chain at the design level:

explanation.text:
[Blue: Place Order] --> [Yellow: Order] --> [Orange: Order Placed]
[Blue: Process Payment] --> [Yellow: Payment] --> [Orange: Payment Authorized]
[Blue: Cancel Order] --> [Yellow: Order] --> [Orange: Order Cancelled]

runs.text: Aggregates are not just data containers — they are consistency boundaries. The yellow sticky represents the rule enforcer: "An order can only be cancelled if it has not yet shipped." Placing yellow stickies forces the team to name their aggregates explicitly and assign command-handling responsibility to them.

Yellow stickies also reveal aggregate boundaries that are poorly drawn. If one yellow sticky appears responsible for three entirely different kinds of commands — taking orders, processing refunds, and managing promotions — that aggregate is likely doing too much. Event Storming makes the smell visible before any code is written.
Aggregates are introduced during design-level event storming, not big-picture storming. Introducing them too early overwhelms participants with technical concepts before the domain is understood.
A yellow sticky is the business object that decides whether a command is allowed. It sits between the request (blue) and what happened (orange) — it is the bouncer that checks the rules.

cards.title: The Lilac Sticky: Policies
cards.teaser: Lilac stickies represent policies — reactive business rules that connect an event to a subsequent command without human intervention. Policies encode the "when X happens, then Y must happen" logic that is often buried in code or tribal knowledge.

runs.text: A
Policy

(sometimes called a Reactor or Process Manager) is a business rule that automatically triggers a command in response to an event. It is written as a conditional statement: "Whenever [Event], then [Command]". Lilac stickies are placed between the event that triggers them and the command they produce.

explanation.text:
[Orange: Payment Failed]
    --> [Lilac: Whenever payment fails, notify the customer]
        --> [Blue: Send Failure Notification]

[Orange: Order Placed]
    --> [Lilac: Whenever an order is placed, reserve inventory]
        --> [Blue: Reserve Inventory]

runs.text: Policies are one of the most revealing elements in an Event Storming session because they make implicit automation explicit. In most codebases, policy logic is buried in service classes, event listeners, or message consumers. During the workshop, domain experts often describe policies verbally — "oh, and when that happens, we also automatically..." — which is the cue for a facilitator to reach for a lilac sticky.

Policies expose coupling between bounded contexts. If a policy says "Whenever an Order is Placed in the Sales context, the Inventory context must Reserve Stock", that is an explicit cross-context dependency that needs to be designed carefully — probably via an asynchronous domain event, not a synchronous call.
A lilac sticky is a business rule that runs on autopilot: when this event occurs, the system automatically fires this command. It is the "if this then that" glue between parts of the domain.

cards.title: The Pink Sticky: External Systems and Hot Spots
cards.teaser: Pink stickies serve double duty: they mark external systems that interact with the domain (payment gateways, email services, third-party APIs) and flag hot spots — areas of confusion, disagreement, or unknown complexity — with a question mark or exclamation mark.

runs.text: In Event Storming,
pink stickies
play two distinct roles depending on context:

items.text: External Systems:

Systems outside the team's control that participate in the domain. A payment gateway that emits "Payment Authorized" events, a shipping carrier API that the system queries, a fraud-detection service that blocks commands. External systems are boundary actors — they issue commands or emit events, but the team cannot change how they behave internally.
Hot Spots:

Areas of friction, uncertainty, or unresolved questions. A hot spot sticky might read "Who owns this?", "Is this really one aggregate or two?", "Legal needs to review", or simply carry a "?". Hot spots are deliberately left unresolved during the session — they are captured, not solved, so momentum is maintained.

runs.text: The hot spot function is one of Event Storming's most practical contributions. In traditional requirements workshops, unresolved questions derail meetings. In Event Storming, they are acknowledged, pinned visibly, and deferred — allowing the session to continue building the overall picture without getting bogged down in a single contested point.

A wall covered in hot spot stickies at the end of a session is not a failure — it is a map of the work that needs to happen before implementation. A wall with no hot spots is a sign the session was not probing deep enough.

Pink stickies flag two things: systems outside your control (the payment processor, the shipping API) and honest question marks ("we don't know who owns this yet"). Both are important precisely because they mark the edges of what is understood.

cards.title: Hot Spots: Surfacing Domain Confusion
cards.teaser: Hot spots are the most intellectually honest element of Event Storming. They mark the spots where the model is wrong, incomplete, contested, or simply unknown. A healthy session produces many hot spots — they are the agenda for follow-up work.

runs.text: Brandolini defines a
hot spot

as any area of the model that raises a concern: a question that cannot be answered in the room, a business rule that experts disagree on, a term that means different things to different people, or a gap in the event timeline that nobody can explain.
Hot spots commonly reveal:

items.text: Naming conflicts.

The sales team calls it a "contract"; the legal team calls it an "agreement". Both are in the room; both have placed orange stickies with different names for the same concept. That tension is a hot spot and a bounded context boundary hint.
Missing domain experts.
A section of the timeline has events that nobody in the room can explain confidently. The hot spot marks that someone who was not invited needs to be brought in.
Invariant disagreements.
Can an order be cancelled after it has shipped? Two domain experts give opposite answers. Hot spot placed — this is a business rule that needs a decision, not a modeling choice.
Complexity flags.

A region of the timeline has dense causality — five events triggering three policies triggering eight commands. The hot spot marks it as a candidate for deeper process-level exploration in a separate session.

runs.text: After the session, hot spots are triaged into: decisions needed, follow-up sessions required, and accepted risks. They become the backlog for domain modeling work.
A hot spot is an honest "we don't know" stuck to the wall in public. It does not stop the workshop — it keeps a record of every unresolved question so they cannot be forgotten.

cards.title: Pivotal Events: Major State Transitions
cards.teaser: Pivotal events are domain events that mark a fundamental change in state — the moment a process crosses a threshold it cannot easily reverse. Identifying them on the timeline structures the entire session and often reveals natural bounded context boundaries.

runs.text: Not all domain events are equal. Some events are minor status updates; others mark a
fundamental transition
in the lifecycle of a business object — a point of no return, a change in ownership, or the triggering of an entirely new set of rules. Brandolini calls these
pivotal events
Examples of pivotal events in an e-commerce domain:

items.text: Order Placed

— the transition from browsing to committed purchase. Before this event, the basket can be changed freely. After it, a whole new set of rules apply: inventory reservation, fraud checks, payment authorization.
Payment Captured
— money has moved. Before this event, cancellation is easy. After it, a refund process must begin.
Shipment Dispatched
— physical goods are in transit. The logistics context now owns the lifecycle. The order context's role changes from "fulfil" to "track".

runs.text: Pivotal events are identified by asking: "Does the set of rules that applies to this object fundamentally change after this event?" If yes, it is pivotal. In Event Storming sessions, pivotal events are sometimes marked with a vertical line across the timeline — a natural chapter break that often corresponds to a bounded context transition.

Pivotal events often map directly to the lifecycle phases visible in the domain's ubiquitous language. When domain experts say "before the order is placed" and "after the order is placed" as a natural distinction, they are signaling a pivotal event.

A pivotal event is the "before and after" moment in a process — after it, the rules change. Identifying them structures the timeline into chapters and often shows where bounded contexts begin and end.

cards.title: Big-Picture Event Storming
cards.teaser: Big-picture event storming is the strategic level — a wide-angle scan of an entire business domain with all stakeholders present. Its goal is not a detailed model but a shared understanding of what happens, where the pain is, and where bounded contexts might live.

runs.text: Big-picture Event Storming is the
exploration phase

: maximum breadth, minimum depth. The format works best with a large, cross-functional group — 10 to 30 people — including domain experts from every part of the business, product managers, and engineers. The goal is to map the entire domain on one very long wall.
Big-picture session structure:

items.text: Chaotic exploration (30-45 minutes):
Everyone writes orange stickies simultaneously and places them on the wall without coordination. Duplicates and conflicts are fine — they are signal.
Timeline ordering (30-45 minutes):
The group arranges stickies into a rough chronological sequence. Disagreements surface. Pivotal events are identified and marked as section boundaries.
Hot spot marking (15-20 minutes):
The group sweeps the timeline and marks every point of confusion, disagreement, or missing knowledge with a hot spot sticky.
Opportunity and value identification (15-20 minutes):
The group marks high-value events — places where the business would benefit most from improvement — often in green. This connects domain modeling to product strategy.

runs.text: Big-picture storming does not produce a domain model. It produces a
landscape

: a shared picture of how the business works, where the problems are, and which areas deserve deeper exploration. Bounded context candidates often emerge naturally as regions of the timeline that cluster around a distinct vocabulary or set of rules.
Big-picture event storming is the wide-angle lens: everyone in the room at once, mapping the whole business. You do not get a precise model — you get a map that shows where the complexity lives.

cards.title: Process-Level Event Storming
cards.teaser: Process-level event storming drills into a single process flow identified during big-picture exploration. It adds commands, policies, and actors to the timeline, producing a detailed picture of one business process without yet specifying the software design.

runs.text: Once big-picture storming has identified a process worth deeper exploration — typically one with many hot spots or high business value — a
process-level session
focuses exclusively on that process. The group is smaller (5-10 people) and more focused: domain experts for that specific area, plus the engineers who will implement it.
Process-level storming introduces elements beyond orange stickies:

items.text: Blue commands
are placed before the events they cause, making the causal chain explicit.
Actors (small yellow person icons or labels)
are placed next to commands to identify who issues them: a customer, a warehouse operator, an automated service.
Lilac policies
are placed between events and the commands they trigger, making automation explicit.
Pink external systems
mark boundaries with third-party services.

runs.text: The result is a detailed narrative of a process: who does what, what happens as a result, which business rules fire automatically, and where external systems interact. This is sufficient to define bounded context APIs, decide on synchronous vs asynchronous integration, and write user stories — without yet specifying aggregate design.

Process-level storming is the sweet spot for cross-team coordination. Two teams whose bounded contexts interact can run a process-level session together to agree on the event contract at their shared boundary before writing a line of code.

Process-level storming takes one slice of the big picture and adds detail: who triggers what, what rules fire automatically, where external systems appear. It answers "how does this process actually work?" without yet answering "how should we code it?"

cards.title: Design-Level Event Storming
cards.teaser: Design-level event storming is the closest to code: aggregates and bounded contexts emerge explicitly. Commands land on aggregates, which enforce invariants and emit events. The output is a model that maps directly to domain objects in the codebase.

runs.text: Design-level Event Storming introduces
yellow aggregate stickies
between blue commands and orange events. The full canonical pattern at the design level is:

explanation.text:
DESIGN-LEVEL TIMELINE

[Actor] --> [Blue: Command] --> [Yellow: Aggregate] --> [Orange: Event]
                                      |                        |
                               enforces invariant          consumed by
                                                        [Lilac: Policy] --> [Blue: Command]

Example: Order Checkout flow

[Customer] --> [Blue: Place Order] --> [Yellow: Order] --> [Orange: Order Placed]
                                           |                       |
                                  checks stock,              [Lilac: on Order Placed,
                                  validates address            reserve inventory]
                                                                       |
                                                            [Blue: Reserve Inventory]
                                                                       |
                                                            [Yellow: Inventory]
                                                                       |
                                                            [Orange: Inventory Reserved]

runs.text: At this level, the session is a small group (3-6 people) of engineers and domain experts. The output maps directly to code:

items.text: Yellow stickies
become aggregate classes with defined consistency boundaries.
Orange stickies
become domain event types, often implemented as immutable value objects.
Blue stickies
become command objects or method calls on aggregates.
Lilac stickies
become event handlers, sagas, or process managers in the application layer.

runs.text: Design-level storming also makes bounded context boundaries sharp. When a command and its handling aggregate seem to belong to a different vocabulary than the surrounding stickies, the session has found a context boundary — the place to draw the line in the code.

Design-level storming adds the yellow aggregate in the middle of every chain: command hits aggregate, aggregate decides if it is allowed, event comes out. After the session you can name your classes directly from the stickies on the wall.

cards.title: The Wall as Canvas
cards.teaser: Event Storming's physical format — an uninterrupted stretch of wall covered in paper, with participants standing and moving around it — is not incidental. The wall is a design tool. Its size enforces breadth; standing prevents the comfortable retreat into slides and monologue.

runs.text: Brandolini's insistence on the wall is deliberate. A standard whiteboard is too small — it invites selective representation and leads to a model that fits within view rather than reflecting the full domain. The minimum recommended canvas for a big-picture session is 8 meters (roughly 25 feet) of uninterrupted wall space, covered with brown paper or a continuous roll of flip-chart paper.
Physical properties of the wall format that matter:

items.text: Breadth creates honesty.
A long wall means you cannot crop the domain to fit. Every part of the process must appear, including the parts nobody wants to talk about.
Standing eliminates hierarchy.
When everyone is on their feet and moving, the conference table power dynamic is broken. The CTO and the junior engineer are equally mobile, equally able to place a sticky.
Sticky notes allow revision without ego.
A sticky can be moved, replaced, or discarded without consequence. There is no "wrong answer" on a whiteboard to be erased in front of everyone — just a note repositioned.
Multiple simultaneous conversations.
A long wall lets 15 people work in parallel across different regions of the timeline without blocking each other. No slide deck supports parallel collaboration.

runs.text: Virtual canvases — Miro, Mural, and the purpose-built
EventModeler

— replicate the mechanics well. EventModeler adds structured notation for commands, events, aggregates, and policies. The main loss in remote Event Storming is the social energy of a shared physical space; skilled remote facilitators compensate with deliberate breakout strategies and camera-on expectations.

The wall is big enough that you cannot fake a complete model — you have to actually map the whole domain. Standing around it, everyone is equal. Stickies can be moved without embarrassment. The format is doing as much work as the technique.

cards.title: Reading an Event Storming Timeline
cards.teaser: An ASCII timeline showing the full vocabulary of Event Storming stickies — commands, aggregates, events, policies, and external systems — is worth more than a written description. Here is the canonical notation and how to read it.

runs.text: The canonical design-level Event Storming timeline, end-to-end for an order fulfillment process:

explanation.text:
TIME ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

[Customer]
    │
    ▼
[BLUE: Place Order]──►[YELLOW: Order]──►[ORANGE: Order Placed]
                            │                      │
                     enforces:                     │
                     - valid items              [LILAC: on Order Placed,
                     - stock available           reserve inventory]
                     - address valid                    │
                                                        ▼
                                               [BLUE: Reserve Inventory]
                                                        │
                                               [YELLOW: Inventory]──►[ORANGE: Inventory Reserved]
                                                                              │
                                                                    [LILAC: on Inventory Reserved,
                                                                     charge payment]
                                                                              │
                                                                              ▼
                                                                    [BLUE: Charge Payment]
                                                                              │
                                                              [PINK: Payment Gateway]
                                                                              │
                                                                    [YELLOW: Payment]──►[ORANGE: Payment Captured]
                                                                                                  │
                                                                                        ──── PIVOTAL EVENT ────
                                                                                                  │
                                                                                        [BLUE: Dispatch Shipment]
                                                                                                  │
                                                                                        [YELLOW: Shipment]──►[ORANGE: Shipment Dispatched]

LEGEND:
  [BLUE]   = Command        (imperative: "Do this")
  [ORANGE] = Domain Event   (past tense: "This happened")
  [YELLOW] = Aggregate      (enforces invariants)
  [LILAC]  = Policy         ("Whenever X, then Y")
  [PINK]   = External System / Hot Spot
  ─── PIVOTAL EVENT ─── = major lifecycle transition

runs.text: Reading this diagram, you can immediately see:

items.text: Three aggregates:
Order, Inventory, Payment, Shipment — candidate bounded contexts or at minimum distinct aggregate roots.
Two policies:
asynchronous chains that could be implemented as domain event handlers.
One external system:
the Payment Gateway, which means an anti-corruption layer is needed.
One pivotal event:
Payment Captured — a before/after threshold with different rules on each side.

runs.text: Reading an Event Storming timeline left to right: blue (someone decided something), yellow (a rule enforcer evaluated it), orange (something happened), lilac (a policy automatically triggered something else). When you see pink, you are crossing a boundary you do not control.

cards.title: The Three Levels in Sequence
cards.teaser: Big-picture, process-level, and design-level are not three independent workshops — they are three resolutions of the same model. Teams start wide and zoom in, using the output of each level as the input for the next.

runs.text: Brandolini designed the three levels to compose into a progressive discovery sequence:

items.text: Level 1 — Big Picture:

"What happens in the whole business?" Outputs: a domain landscape, candidate bounded contexts marked by pivotal events and vocabulary clusters, and a prioritized list of hot spots and high-value areas to explore further.
Level 2 — Process:

"How does this specific process work?" Takes one high-value area from the big picture and adds commands, actors, policies, and external system touchpoints. Outputs: a detailed process flow, agreed event contracts at context boundaries, and the information architecture for user stories.
Level 3 — Design:

"What are the aggregates and their invariants?" Takes one process flow and adds yellow aggregate stickies. Outputs: named aggregates with their commands and events, bounded context boundaries, and a design that maps to code structure.

runs.text: Not every feature requires all three levels. A simple CRUD feature with no domain complexity might skip directly to design-level. A major new domain area — the first time a company enters a new market, for example — warrants all three, run in sequence over several days.

The three-level structure also maps to team topologies. Big-picture involves all stakeholders. Process-level is a cross-team session between the teams that own connected bounded contexts. Design-level is a single team's internal modeling session.

The most common mistake is skipping straight to design-level without big-picture exploration. Teams that do this build the right software for the wrong domain — they model what they already understand instead of discovering what they do not.

The three levels are zoom levels on the same map. Start wide (what does the whole business do?), then zoom in on one process (how exactly does this work?), then zoom in again on the objects (what enforces the rules?). Each session feeds the next.

cards.title: Outcomes: What Event Storming Produces
cards.teaser: Event Storming's tangible outputs are bounded context discovery, a shared ubiquitous language, model alignment across teams, and a map of domain complexity that guides architectural decisions. These outcomes persist long after the sticky notes come down.

runs.text: Event Storming produces five categories of lasting output:

items.text: Bounded Context Discovery.

Regions of the timeline with consistent vocabulary, distinct aggregates, and clear pivotal event boundaries become bounded context candidates. This is often the most direct path to a context map that would otherwise take weeks of architecture meetings.
Ubiquitous Language.

Every orange sticky is a term that both domain experts and engineers have agreed on, in writing, in public. Naming conflicts discovered during the session ("you call it an agreement, we call it a contract") are resolved into a shared vocabulary. This language goes directly into code.
Model Alignment.

Engineers often have a mental model of the domain based on a data model or an old API. Domain experts have a model based on how the business actually works. Event Storming forces these models to confront each other. The mismatches are often profound — and finding them in a workshop is far cheaper than finding them in a production incident.
Complexity Map.

The hot spot distribution reveals where the domain is well-understood (few hot spots, clear vocabulary) versus where it is contested or complex (dense hot spots, naming conflicts). This complexity map informs architectural decisions: high-complexity regions deserve richer domain models; simple regions can use simpler patterns.
Integration Contracts.

Events at bounded context boundaries — visible on the timeline as orange stickies that flow from one vocabulary cluster into another — become the proposed integration contracts between teams. They can be formalized as consumer-driven contracts immediately after the session.

runs.text: Brandolini describes Event Storming not as a one-time activity but as a
continuous practice

. Teams that run Event Storming sessions regularly — at the start of each major feature area, when domain complexity escalates, or when teams need to align on a shared boundary — build a cumulative model of their domain that becomes one of the organization's most valuable assets.

Photograph the wall before it comes down. The photograph is a lightweight, shareable artifact of the session's output. For remote sessions, export the canvas as a PDF or image immediately — virtual canvases do not survive link rot.

After Event Storming, you walk away with named bounded contexts, agreed vocabulary that goes straight into code, a map of where the hard problems are, and proposed event contracts between teams. The sticky notes come down; the shared understanding does not.
